evidence: Plin. NH 8.76: ūnō cornū nigrō mediā fronte cubitōrum duūm ēminente (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Pliny’s fierce beast of India, with a horse’s body, a stag’s head, an elephant’s feet, a boar’s tail, a deep bellow, and a single black horn two cubits long standing out from the middle of its forehead. The white horned horse of the fairy tales is a later picture; the word serves for it.

terms.gloss: the unicorn of the Latin Bible
evidence: Vulg. Ps. 91 (92), 11: sīcut ūnicornis cornū meum
terms.comment: As a noun in the Vulgate’s psalms; classically an adjective, “one-horned” (Plin. NH 8.72, of Indian oxen, Lewis & Short). Morgan–Owens gives it for the imaginary unicorn.

phrases.latin: Ecce monocerōs, cui ūnum cornū ē mediā fronte ēminet.
phrases.english: Look, a unicorn, with a single horn sticking out of the middle of its forehead.

phrases.latin: asperrimam autem feram monocerōtem, reliquō corpore equō similem, capite cervō, pedibus elephantō, caudā aprō, mūgītū gravī, ūnō cornū nigrō mediā fronte cubitōrum duūm ēminente
phrases.english: but the fiercest beast is the unicorn, like a horse in the rest of its body, a stag in its head, an elephant in its feet, a boar in its tail, with a deep bellow and one black horn two cubits long standing out from the middle of its forehead

phrases.latin: et exaltābitur sīcut ūnicornis cornū meum
phrases.english: and my horn shall be raised up like a unicorn’s

sources: Lewis & Short: monoceros · Lewis & Short: unicornis
